title: Telling Time, Dates, and Simple Plans
goal: Tell clock times, read dates, and make simple plans in Norwegian.

objectives.statement: Tell clock times, read dates, and make simple plans in Norwegian.

spans.value: Nora and Amir have registered for an evening Norwegian course. Nora has the confirmation message open on her phone, but she wants to make sure that she has understood the date and time correctly.
Nora:
Når begynner norskkurset?

blocks.translation: When does the Norwegian course begin?

spans.value: Amir:
Tirsdag 14. mai.
Nora:
Er det den fjortende?
Amir:
Ja. Det begynner klokka halv seks.

blocks.translation: Yes. It begins at half past five.

spans.value: Nora:
Halv seks? Altså 17.30?

blocks.translation: Half past five? In other words, 17:30?

spans.value: Amir:
Ja. Skal vi møtes et kvarter før?

blocks.translation: Yes. Shall we meet a quarter of an hour earlier?

spans.value: Nora:
Gjerne. Passer kvart over fem?

blocks.translation: Gladly. Does quarter past five work?

spans.value: Amir:
Ja, vi møtes ved inngangen klokka kvart over fem.

blocks.translation: Yes, we’ll meet by the entrance at quarter past five.

spans.value: Nora:
Flott. Da ses vi tirsdag den fjortende mai.

blocks.translation: Great. Then I’ll see you on Tuesday, the fourteenth of May.

spans.value: The important moment in this conversation is Nora’s reaction to halv seks. Norwegian tells half hours differently from English. Norwegian halv seks means halfway toward six, so it is 5:30, not 6:30.
The conversation also shows two ways to express the date. A written notice may show 14. mai, while the date is read aloud as den fjortende mai or simply fjortende mai.
Finally, Nora and Amir use the time and date to make a simple plan. They confirm when the course begins and choose an earlier meeting time.
To ask what time it is, Norwegian commonly uses:
Klokka is the definite form of klokke, meaning clock. Klokken is also correct, but klokka is very common in everyday Bokmål.
To give an exact hour, use klokka er followed by the number.
You can add presis when you mean exactly on the hour.
When the sentence already contains another verb, klokka introduces the time.

en.value: The course begins at six o’clock.
The bus leaves at eight o’clock.

spans.value: English normally uses at before a clock time. Norwegian usually does not use a separate preposition here: klokka itself introduces the time.
Compare:
Not:
The Norwegian sentence does not need på before klokka.

sections.title: Minutes after and before the hour

spans.value: Use over for minutes after an hour.
Kvart means a quarter. The expression kvart over fem therefore means a quarter after five: 5:15.
Use på for minutes before the next hour.
A useful way to understand på is to look forward to the coming hour:
The hour named after på is the hour that is approaching.
An aligned contrast
Notice that the named hour changes after the half-hour. At 5:45, Norwegian looks toward six, so the expression is kvart på seks.

sections.title: The half hour: looking toward the next hour

spans.value: Norwegian half-hour expressions look forward to the next hour.
Literally, halv seks is half toward six. The time is therefore 5:30.
Compare the pattern:
This is one of the most important differences between Norwegian and English time-telling.
A common mistake is to translate each word directly and interpret halv seks as half past six. That would give the wrong time by one hour. Instead, ask: Which hour are we halfway toward?

en.value: The film begins at half past eight.
The train leaves at half past one.
We eat dinner at half past six.

sections.title: Times close to the half hour

spans.value: Norwegian can also count minutes before or after the half-hour.

no.value: Klokka er fem på halv seks.

spans.value: This is five minutes before halv seks, so it is 5:25.

no.value: Klokka er fem over halv seks.

spans.value: This is five minutes after halv seks, so it is 5:35.

no.value: Klokka er ti på halv seks.
Klokka er ti over halv seks.

spans.value: The logic remains consistent:

items.value: Before the half-hour, count toward halv plus the next hour.
After the half-hour, count from halv plus the next hour.

spans.value: These forms are common in everyday conversation. At first, it can help to locate halv seks at 5:30 and then move backward or forward by the stated number of minutes.
Norwegian schedules often use the 24-hour clock in writing.
In speech, you may read a formal timetable time with the 24-hour numbers.

en.value: The train leaves at seventeen thirty.
The meeting begins at fourteen fifteen.

spans.value: In ordinary conversation, speakers often use the twelve-hour expressions when the context makes morning or evening clear.

en.value: The train leaves at quarter past eight.
The meeting begins at quarter past two.

spans.value: Nora uses both systems to check the same time:

en.value: Half past five? In other words, 17:30?

spans.value: This is a useful checking strategy when a spoken time might be misunderstood.
Norwegian normally writes the day before the month.
Month names are normally written with a lowercase letter:
The full stop after the day number is important. It shows that the number is an ordinal number: first, second, third, and so on.
A written date such as 14. mai is therefore read with an ordinal number:
You may also hear den before the date.
Both forms can occur in complete sentences:

en.value: The course begins on the fourteenth of May.
The course begins on the fourteenth of May.

spans.value: Useful ordinal forms for dates include:
The written number and the spoken form do different jobs. You write 14. but say fjortende. Do not normally read it as the cardinal number fjorten when it represents a date.
Compare:
The first sentence uses the cardinal number fjorten because it counts books. The date is read fjortende because it identifies the fourteenth day of the month.
To ask for a calendar date, use:
To ask when an event happens, use når.
A weekday can appear before the date.

en.value: The course begins on Tuesday, 14 May.

spans.value: When a weekday is used by itself to identify a day, på is common.
With a full written schedule, the date may follow directly.
Clock times and dates become useful when you arrange to do something.
A common suggestion is:
Add a day, date, or time to make the plan more specific.

no.value: Skal vi møtes fredag 12. juni klokka tre?

en.value: Shall we meet on Friday, 12 June, at three?

spans.value: To ask whether a proposed time is suitable, use passer.
Useful short responses include:
After agreement, confirm the plan clearly.

no.value: Da møtes vi klokka halv fire.

en.value: Then we’ll meet at half past three.

no.value: Vi møtes fredag 12. juni klokka halv fire.

en.value: We’ll meet on Friday, 12 June, at half past three.

spans.value: The confirmation matters because it puts the day, date, and time together in one clear plan.
Nora checks the course message one more time.
Nora:
Kurset begynner tirsdag 14. mai klokka 17.30.

blocks.translation: The course begins on Tuesday, 14 May, at 17:30.

spans.value: Amir:
Ja, altså halv seks.

blocks.translation: Yes, in other words, half past five.

spans.value: Nora:
Og vi møtes kvart over fem?

blocks.translation: And we’re meeting at quarter past five?

spans.value: Amir:
Ja. Vi møtes ved inngangen klokka kvart over fem.

blocks.translation: Yes. We’ll meet by the entrance at quarter past five.

spans.value: Nora:
Bra. Da har vi god tid før kurset begynner.

blocks.translation: Good. Then we have plenty of time before the course begins.

spans.value: Nora now moves confidently between the written schedule and the everyday spoken time. She also repeats the meeting time, giving Amir a chance to confirm it. Their plan is clear: Tuesday, 14 May, at 5:15, before the course begins at 5:30.

en.value: 'Not: half past six (for this Norwegian phrase)'

spans.value: Correct interpretation:
Norwegian names the next hour in a half-hour expression.

Incorrect interpretation:

en.value: 'Not: quarter past six (for this Norwegian phrase)'

spans.value: Correct interpretation:
På points toward the approaching hour.

Less natural for the date:
Standard date reading:
The written date 14. mai represents an ordinal day.

Incorrect:
Correct:
Use på with a weekday such as på fredag, but use klokka directly before a clock time.

prompt.value: Classify each Norwegian schedule sentence by direction around the named hour: after the hour with over, or before the hour with på.

explanation.value: Clock expressions are calculated around the coming hour: halv seks is 17:30, and over/på/før place minutes relative to the named hour.
